extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate students in combinatorics/graph theory and mathematically literate readers
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapters presenting combinatorics and graph-theory theorems (partitions identities, Euler/pentagonal theorem, Rogers–Ramanujan remarks, five-/list-coloring of planar graphs, art-gallery theorem, Turán's theorem) together with proofs, constructions and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line graph equality conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Does x(H) = x_e(H) hold for every line graph H? (Here x denotes chromatic number, x_e the list-chromatic number.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: x(H)=x_e(H) holds when H is the line graph of a bipartite graph (adaptation of earlier proof). Conjectured more generally for all line graphs H; currently open and hard. Example counterpoint: not every graph is a line graph (e.g., K2,4), and x(K2,4) < x_e(K2,4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition generating-function identity (unrestricted partitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The infinite product ∏_{k≥1} (1 + x^k + x^{2k} + x^{3k} + ...) = ∏_{k≥1} 1/(1 - x^k) expands to ∑_{n≥0} p(n) x^n, where p(n) counts partitions of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: coefficient of x^n equals the number of ways to write n as a sum of positive integers (order disregarded). Use factor k to account for multiplicity of part k. Example: p(5)=7 with listed partitions. This identity is a basic combinatorial encoding of partition counts by formal power series; convergence issues are ignored in formal-series treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partitions into odd parts = partitions into distinct parts (p_o(n)=p_d(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity ∏_{k≥1} (1/(1 - x^{2k-1})) = ∏_{k≥1} (1 + x^k) implies p_o(n) = p_d(n) for all n > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial meaning: left product counts partitions into odd summands, right product counts partitions into distinct summands. Glaisher's bijection (1907) provides an explicit bijection: write multiplicities of odd parts in binary and transform 2^r multiplicities into scaled distinct parts. Example mapping given (25 = 5+5+5+3+3+1+1+1+1 → 10+6+5+4). The bijection is invertible by collecting parts by highest power of 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct-parts / 1±x^k formal-product interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: The product ∏_{k≥1} (1 + x^k) expands to a series whose coefficient of x^n equals p_d(n), the number of partitions of n into distinct summands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take either 1 or x^k from each factor, so each k appears at most once. Removing factors corresponds to forbidding that summand. Useful for deriving combinatorial equalities by algebraic manipulation (e.g., pairing cancellations when using 1 - x^2 = (1 - x)(1 + x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's pentagonal theorem (coefficients of ∏(1 - x^k))
rubrics_metrics.description: The infinite product ∏_{k≥1} (1 - x^k) expands to a series whose coefficients are 0, +1 or -1 and nonzero terms occur at generalized pentagonal numbers b(j)=3j^2−j over j∈Z, with signs alternating by parity of j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation of exponents sequence 1,5,12,22,35,51,70,... (pentagonal numbers). Proofs may proceed via formal power-series manipulation or bijection/involution constructions. The Bressoud–Zeilberger involution provides a clean combinatorial proof constructing a map between partitions contributing to cancelations and producing the claimed recurrence/coefficients. Use c(0)=1 and recurrence ∑_{k=0}^n c(k) p(n−k)=0 to identify coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bressoud–Zeilberger involution for Euler's identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an involution φ on partitions that maps partitions of n−b(j) to either partitions of n−b(j−1) or n−b(j+1), so as to establish the pentagonal recurrence and coefficient pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: for X = λ1+...+λt ∈ P(n−b(j)), transform by case distinction comparing t+3j and λ1 and adjusting parts accordingly (increase/decrease parts, drop zeros). The map is an involution and shows the requisite cancellations to produce Euler's coefficient sequence. Example given for n=15, j=2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rogers–Ramanujan identities and partition bijection goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Two infinite-product identities (Rogers–Ramanujan) imply partition equalities: (1) partitions with parts ≡1,4 (mod 5) equal partitions with parts differing by at least 2, (2) partitions with parts ≡2,3 (mod 5) equal partitions with parts differing by at least 2 and without 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All known formal-series proofs are involved; bijective proofs existed (Garsia–Milne, 1981) but are complicated; 'Book proofs' via simple bijections remain elusive. The text invites translation of product identities into partition statements (MacMahon) and notes historical context (Rogers, Ramanujan) and known bijection results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-coloring plane graphs via Euler's formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Every plane graph is 6-colorable: remove a vertex of degree ≤5 (existence follows from Euler's formula and planar graph properties), color remaining graph by induction, then color removed vertex with a color different from its ≤5 neighbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction on n: base trivial for small n. Use fact from planar graph properties that some vertex has degree ≤5. This simple argument extends to list-coloring (list size 6) to obtain x_e(G) ≤ 6. Example and step-by-step induction given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thomassen's 5-list-colorability theorem (strong induction hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: All planar graphs G are 5-choosable: more precisely, for a near-triangulated plane graph G with outer cycle B, if two adjacent vertices of B are precolored with different colors and every other vertex v of B has |C(v)|>3 and every interior vertex has |C(v)|>5, then the coloring can be extended by choosing colors from lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses induction with two cases: (I) B has a chord—split into two near-triangulated parts and apply induction; (II) B has no chord—remove suitable interior vertex v0, reduce neighbor lists by two chosen colors from C(v0), and apply induction on the resulting near-triangulated graph G'. The assumptions (1)-(3) are the induction hypothesis and are crucial to ensuring extendability. Conclusion: x_e(G) ≤ 5. The proof does not use Euler's formula and illustrates the choice of a stronger induction hypothesis to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples to x_e(G) ≤ x(G) + 1 for planar graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjecture x_e(G) ≤ x(G) + 1 (for planar graphs) fails in Case II (x(G)=3): explicit planar graphs exist with x(G)=3 and x_e(G)=5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction outline: Gutner's 130-vertex graph assembled from 16 copies of a 'double-octahedron' gadget (with specified lists per figure) yields a planar 3-colorable graph that is not 4-choosable; Voigt and Wirth constructed smaller examples (75 vertices), current record 63 vertices, demonstrating x_e(G) can be 5 while x(G)=3. These are constructive counterexamples showing the conjecture is false in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art gallery theorem (floor(n/3) guards suffice)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any simple polygon (museum) with n walls (vertices), ⌊n/3⌋ guards stationed at vertices suffice to see every point of the museum interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof (Fisk): triangulate polygon (n−3 noncrossing diagonals), view as plane graph, 3-color triangulation, and place guards on smallest color class (≤⌊n/3⌋ vertices). Justification of triangulation existence is by induction using convex vertices and selecting diagonals (sliding argument). Example comb-shaped museum shows lower bound of ⌊n/3⌋ is tight in worst case. Variants are discussed (guards along walls, vertex guards, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation existence for simple polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simple (planar, non-self-intersecting) polygon can be triangulated by a finite set of noncrossing diagonals (induction on n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key step: polygon has at least three convex vertices; pick a convex vertex A and check its neighbors B and C: if BC inside polygon it's a diagonal, otherwise slide BC toward A until it hits last vertex Z in triangle ABC' and AZ is a diagonal. This yields smaller polygons for induction. Note: the analogous 3D generalization fails (Schonhardt's polyhedron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-gallery variants: wall-guards and lower bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Variant problem: guards patrol edges (wall-guards) and see everything visible from some point of their assigned wall; there are polygons requiring as many as ~n/4 wall-guards (example by Toussaint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Toussaint constructed a polygon with 28 sides that requires 7 wall-guards (in general 4m sides yield m wall-guards), giving large lower bounds (example with 171 guards cited). It is conjectured that (except small n) this number might also be sufficient, but no proof (Book proof) is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turán's theorem (extremal edge bound without p-clique)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a simple graph on n vertices with no p-clique (p>2), then the maximum number of edges is attained by the Turán graph (complete (p−1)-partite graph with part sizes as equal as possible) and equals (1−1/(p−1)) n^2/2 (equivalently the exact balanced-part formula given in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: divide vertex set into p−1 parts V_1,...,V_{p-1}, join across parts (no edges inside parts); balancing part sizes maximizes edges. The theorem asserts this bound is an upper bound for any p-clique-free graph and that Turán graphs are (essentially) unique maximizers. Special cases: p=3 yields Mantel's theorem (triangle-free bound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction proof of Turán (Erdős/Turán style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by induction on n: take a (p−1)-clique A, let B = V ackslash A, use induction to bound edges inside B and observe each vertex of B can be adjacent to at most p−2 vertices in A, summing to obtain Turán bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: existence of (p−1)-cliques in an extremal graph, counting e_A,B ≤ (p−2)(n−p+1), and using induction bound on e(B). Yields explicit algebraic inequality equal to Turán's bound. Useful as a classical combinatorial proof approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Max-degree / multipartite-structure proof of Turán
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct graph H by taking vertex v of maximum degree, let S be its neighbors and T the rest, then alter graph to move all edges to be between S and T (T independent), apply induction on S and conclude extremal graphs must be complete multipartite (Turán graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique shows among all extremal graphs there exists one of the 'H' form; induction bounds edges in S, combined with full bipartite connections to T give Turán bound. This also suggests uniqueness characterization leading to complete multipartite structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motzkin–Straus (maximization) approach to Turán
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a probability distribution w=(w1,...,wn) on vertices and maximize f(w)=∑_{i<j, ij∈E} w_i w_j. Optimal distributions concentrate weights on a clique, and maximizing yields an inequality f(w) ≤ (1−1/(p−1))/2 for p−1 clique-size limit, which applied to uniform weights gives Turán's bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: perform weight-shifting to eliminate positive weights on non-adjacent vertices until weights concentrate on a clique; further smoothing shows equal weights on clique maximize f; evaluate for k≤p−1 to obtain bound. This analytic method links continuous optimization with extremal combinatorics (Motzkin–Straus theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic permutation method (Alon–Spencer style) for clique lower bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a random permutation of vertices and let C_π be set of vertices that appear before all their non-neighbors; the expected size E|C_π| = ∑_{i=1}^n 1/(n−d_i) gives a lower bound on clique number ω(G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute indicator variables for each vertex being 'first among its non-neighbors' in permutation; linearity of expectation yields expected clique size. Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to transform this lower bound into an inequality that, combined with assumption ω(G) ≤ p−1, yields Turán's edge bound. This is a probabilistic combinatorics proof method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness via duplication/structure argument (complete multipartite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremal graphs achieving Turán's edge bound cannot contain a triple u,v,w with vw∈E but neither uv nor uw in E; duplicating higher-degree vertices and deleting lower-degree ones leads to contradictions unless the graph is complete multipartite, hence Turán graphs are unique maximizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-case duplication argument: if degree comparisons favor replacements, duplicating certain vertices and deleting others increases edge count unless forbidden structure is absent. The forbidden triple condition is equivalent to partition-equivalence relation; conclusion: extremal graph is complete multipartite K_{n1,...,n_{p-1}} with balanced parts.
